endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The AI materially changes the standard of care or substitutes for clinician judgment in a discrete decision.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: The oncologist reviews the report and discusses it with the patient to select a personalized treatment, such as a clinical trial and/or an approved or guideline-recommended therapeutic regimen intervention(s), in the context of supporting evidence, potential benefits and possible risks.

endorsements.title: Legal implications of AI standard of care integration on patients’ informed consent: lessons from surgery
endorsements.quote: In addition to information about recognized risks that are reasonably expected to impact the planned treatment, patients should also receive information about unknown risks of experimental treatments as well as viable alternative treatments, particularly when they present different risk profiles th an the chosen treatment .

endorsements.title: Clinician in the loop: a flawed solution for AI oversight
endorsements.quote: Instead, they should support explicit discussion of AI outputs, their validity, and their limits, enabling patients and clinicians to co-create care plans.

endorsements.title: Humanoid robots in the operating room: a framework for staged integration of embodied AI in surgery
endorsements.quote: Informed consent must clearly define the functional scope, level of autonomy, and potential risks to patient safety posed by deployed humanoids in the OR, thereby enabling open discussion and mitigating hesitation toward autonomous medical AI46,47.

endorsements.title: Ethical challenges and evolving strategies in the integration of artificial intelligence into clinical practice
endorsements.quote: Patients must know and understand the process behind healthcare decisions made by AI, and require care givers to explain to patients the limitations and reason for such AI-driven decisions [ 33 ].

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Plastic Surgery
endorsements.issuer: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
endorsements.quote: Patients should be given AI-generated recommendations and alternative options, ensuring they understand their right to accept or decline AI tools.

endorsements.title: Responsible artificial intelligence integration framework for psychiatric guidelines
endorsements.quote: Transparent patient communication is likewise essential; where algorithmic reasoning influences treatment options, it must be explainable in conceptually intelligible terms that preserve trust and autonomy.

endorsements.title: The clinician as gatekeeper in the age of "deep research"
endorsements.quote: A pragmatic norm would be to disclose AI involvement in plain language and to confirm understanding with a brief teach-back.

endorsements.title: Risk and liability in the deployment of AI systems for surgery: a SAGES white paper
endorsements.quote: Furthermore, surgeons should be equipped to have a discussion on reasonable alternatives to not using AI assistance in a patient’s care, offering data on how care might be different or whether there are any expected differences in outcome due to not using an AI system.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in traumatic stress treatment: The TRUST framework for ethical development, clinical applications, and research advancement
endorsements.quote: Central to such a framework is the implementation of transparent, informed consent processes that explicitly detail the extent of AI involvement in a survivor’s clinical care or research participation.

endorsements.title: A Human-Governed Clinical Informatics Framework for Safe AI-Assisted Mental Health Counseling: Secondary Framework Development and Requirement Mapping Study
endorsements.quote: In supervised pilot settings, institutions should disclose to patients or clients when AI-generated draft summaries or risk support tools are used in documentation, triage, or the counseling workflow while clarifying that final interpretation and decisions remain the responsibility of a qualified human professional.

commentary.bottom_line: Nine sources endorse discussing evidence, benefits, risks, and non-AI alternatives with patients when AI materially shapes a clinical recommendation, but no supplied study tests whether such discussions change patient understanding, decisions, or outcomes. No supplied study documents how often patients accept AI-influenced recommendations without this information.

perspectives.view: The endorsements come from two CHAI frameworks and seven commentaries, and none reports primary data. No study tests the practice, and no study measures the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the level of agreement among sources reflects expert opinion rather than tested effect.

One commentary proposes plain-language disclosure with a brief teach-back, and the SAGES white paper asks surgeons to offer data on outcomes without AI. No supplied study measures the time these conversations take, how consistently clinicians deliver them, or whether comparative outcome data exist to support the alternatives discussion.

Several sources frame the discussion as protecting patients' right to accept or decline AI tools and to know a qualified human remains responsible for decisions. Whether patients experience these conversations as informative or as added burden has not been studied in the supplied evidence.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare structured AI-disclosure and alternatives discussions against usual care, measuring patient comprehension, decisional conflict, uptake of AI-influenced recommendations, clinician time, and downstream outcomes. Baseline studies should also establish how often AI materially influences recommendations without patient awareness.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The teach-back and plain-language approaches proposed in one commentary may matter most for these groups, but their feasibility with interpreters and their effect on comprehension in these populations remain unknown.
